text: A finished card on a Kanban board isn't the same thing as a change that's safely live for real users. Between writing the code and customers using it sits a chain of environments, each one answering a different question about whether the change is actually safe to ship.

Dev is where a change is written and debugged — it answers does this work at all. QA tests the change systematically against expected behavior and edge cases — does this work correctly, including cases the developer didn't think of. UAT is the actual business trying it out — is this what we actually wanted. And Production is the live system — nothing reaches it until every stage before it has passed.

That DEV to QA to UAT to PROD chain compresses a lot of real steps into one box. Inside Dev alone: a ticket is assigned from the sprint backlog, a branch is created so the work stays isolated, a teammate code-reviews the pull request, and only after merging does testing in QA even begin.

Each environment also has a different person in the driver's seat. A problem in Dev is the developer's own to fix. A problem in QA is a QA engineer's or test suite's job to catch. If the business rejects something in UAT, that's not a bug — it's a sign the requirements need another look. And once something's in Production, it's everyone's problem, which is exactly why the chain exists.
